name: ZIM Connections
tagline: A consumer eSIM platform in production: React Native apps, white-label web platforms, a NestJS backend and AWS infrastructure.

sources.label: ZIM eSIM on the App Store

overview.text: A consumer eSIM platform selling international data, calls and connectivity plans, with paying customers.
The platform includes a React Native app on iOS and Android, white-label web platforms for partner brands including Swiss Federal Railways (SBB), SoftBank and Akwaaba, and a business dashboard.

Over Alex's time there the platform grew from under 1,000 to 50,000+ users and from a single application to a multi-brand ecosystem. This was a team effort by a small engineering team that Alex was part of.

responsibilities.text: Worked autonomously within a small, fast-moving engineering team, owning features from technical design through deployment and production support.
Maintained the production TypeScript/Node.js/NestJS API, which served 5.4M requests in six months at a 99.9% non-5xx rate and a 104 ms median response time.

Owned the design, development and production rollout of the platform's real-time live chat, covering the Socket.IO/NestJS/React Native gateway, services, database schema, rate limiting and shared React client hooks. As of September 2026 it supported 5,000+ conversations and 100,000+ messages.
Grew backend automated testing to 2,623 tests across 88 suites, reaching 61% statement coverage, and established the core API's CI/CD test gate.
Collaborated with another developer to design and implement ZIM's multi-tenant architecture, supporting four production brands and eleven application identities on shared infrastructure.

Managed containerised (Docker) production services on AWS across 13 CloudFront distributions, Application Load Balancers, RDS and networking, supporting millions of monthly requests across customer and partner applications.
Built frontend features in the React Native app and customer and B2B dashboards in React and Next.js.
Helped scale the platform from under 1,000 to 50,000+ users and from a single application to a multi-brand ecosystem.

overview.text: The backend is a set of separately deployed and separately reviewed Node.js services: a NestJS API, an Express provider connector and a notifications service. They communicate over REST, and over WebSockets (Socket.IO) where clients need updates pushed rather than polled.

The NestJS API runs on EC2 in private subnets with no public IP address. It is reachable only through an Application Load Balancer, behind Amazon CloudFront and AWS WAF, with Cloudflare as authoritative DNS.
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL runs Multi-AZ with a synchronous standby, automated failover and point-in-time recovery.
Amazon Cognito issues user tokens. IAM instance profiles and STS supply short-lived, automatically rotated service credentials, and Secrets Manager holds the remaining secrets.
Lambda and SQS handle background work that should not block a request; SNS and SES send push notifications and email.
Elastic APM and browser RUM report traces, errors and latency into Kibana.
As of the September 2026 CV, one codebase was themed for 4 brands and 11 app identities, and the live chat's shared React hooks were used by both the mobile app and the web.

challenges.title: Real-time live chat across mobile and web
challenges.problem: Customer conversations needed messages pushed to clients rather than polled, on both the React Native app and the web.
approach: A Socket.IO gateway on the NestJS backend, with its own services, database schema and rate limiting.
Shared React client hooks used by both the mobile app and the web clients.
challenges.outcome: Rolled out to production; as of September 2026 it supported 5,000+ conversations and 100,000+ messages.

challenges.title: Serving many brands without forking the product
challenges.problem: The platform moved from a single application to several partner brands and app identities.
approach: A multi-tenant architecture on shared infrastructure.
Partner-specific behaviour is kept out of the core, so adding a partner is a configuration change rather than a fork.
challenges.outcome: As of the September 2026 CV, 4 production brands and 11 app identities ran on shared infrastructure.

challenges.title: Confidence to ship changes to a production API
challenges.problem: A production API with paying customers needs changes verified before they reach users.
approach: Grew the backend automated test suite to 2,623 tests across 88 suites (61% statement coverage).
Established a CI/CD test gate on the core API, so changes merge only when the suite passes.

decisions.title: Short-lived credentials instead of stored keys
decisions.decision: Services obtain credentials from IAM instance profiles and STS, which rotate them automatically, and Secrets Manager holds everything else.
decisions.rationale: No long-lived key sits on disk.

decisions.title: Background work off the request path
decisions.decision: Lambda and SQS handle work that should never block a request.
decisions.rationale: Keeps request latency independent of slow or retryable background jobs.

decisions.title: WebSockets only where pushing is needed
decisions.decision: Services talk over REST, with Socket.IO WebSockets used where the client needs pushing rather than polling.
decisions.rationale: Clients get real-time updates where they matter, such as live chat, without moving every interaction to a persistent connection.

decisions.title: Partner behaviour in configuration, not in the core
decisions.decision: Partner-specific behaviour is kept out of the shared core.
decisions.rationale: Adding the next partner should be a configuration change rather than a fork.

lessons.text: The interesting engineering in white-labelling is not the theming but keeping partner-specific behaviour out of the core.

limitations.text: This is employer-owned work. The source code is private, so details here come from Alex's CV and public descriptions of the platform.
